authors: J. G. Wardrop
title: Some Theoretical Aspects of Road Traffic Research
venue: Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers
impact: Seminal: foundation of user-equilibrium and system-optimum reasoning.
problem: How self-interested route choice differs from a system-wide optimum.
takeaway: Governance must distinguish user equilibrium from system optimum; route guidance or pricing that only shifts users among routes can fail if it ignores network equilibrium.
use: Use when evaluating diversion, route guidance, pricing, network design, or Braess-type effects.
caution: Static equilibrium does not capture queue spillback, temporal dynamics, or incident recovery.

authors: D. Braess, A. Nagurney, T. Wakolbinger
title: On a Paradox of Traffic Planning
impact: Highly cited English presentation of the Braess paradox; Transportation Science.
problem: Why adding a link can worsen equilibrium travel times.
takeaway: Capacity expansion is not automatically congestion relief; always test equilibrium rerouting and network-wide performance after topology changes.
use: Use for road additions, lane additions, turn openings, reversible links, and route guidance.
caution: The paradox is topology- and cost-function-dependent; do not claim every new road worsens traffic.

authors: W. S. Vickrey
title: Congestion Theory and Transport Investment
problem: How congestion externalities should affect pricing and investment.
takeaway: Congestion is partly a pricing and scheduling problem, not only a capacity problem; marginal-cost logic is a core governance principle.
use: Use for peak pricing, toll design, demand spreading, and investment appraisal.
caution: Pure efficiency pricing must be paired with equity, acceptability, and implementation analysis.

authors: K. A. Small
title: The Scheduling of Consumer Activities: Work Trips
problem: How travelers trade travel time against early/late arrival penalties.
takeaway: Peak congestion can be governed by shifting departure times as well as routes or modes; schedule delay is part of generalized cost.
use: Use for staggered work hours, peak spreading, dynamic pricing, and bottleneck analysis.
caution: Behavioral parameters are context-dependent and should be calibrated when quantitative recommendations are made.

authors: R. Arnott, A. de Palma, R. Lindsey
title: A Structural Model of Peak-Period Congestion: A Traffic Bottleneck with Elastic Demand
impact: Seminal structural bottleneck model; major reference in congestion economics.
problem: Peak-period equilibrium when demand is elastic and queueing is endogenous.
takeaway: Policies affect not only queues but whether, when, and how much people travel; demand response must be included in governance evaluation.
use: Use for dynamic congestion pricing and peak-period policy design.
caution: Point-bottleneck abstraction omits network spillback and multi-intersection interactions.

authors: C. F. Daganzo
title: The Cell Transmission Model: A Dynamic Representation of Highway Traffic Consistent with the Hydrodynamic Theory
impact: Seminal dynamic traffic-flow paper; one of the most cited TR-B traffic-flow works.
problem: Represent queue formation, propagation, and dissipation with a computationally tractable model.
takeaway: Governance decisions must respect finite storage and shock propagation; average speed alone can hide spillback and blocking.
use: Use for dynamic bottlenecks, incidents, lane closures, evacuation, and simulation reasoning.
caution: Cell size/time step and fundamental-diagram assumptions matter; it is a macroscopic approximation.

authors: C. F. Daganzo
title: The Cell Transmission Model, Part II: Network Traffic
problem: Dynamic multi-commodity flows through network junctions.
takeaway: Network control should model node interactions, turn proportions, and downstream receiving capacity rather than treating links independently.
use: Use for network simulation, DTA, evacuation, diversion, and queue-spillback analysis.
caution: Junction rules and route-choice assumptions must match the intended application.

authors: M. Papageorgiou
title: Dynamic Modeling, Assignment, and Route Guidance in Traffic Networks
impact: Influential early integration of dynamic assignment, guidance, and control.
problem: How route guidance interacts with dynamic network traffic.
takeaway: Information is a control input: guidance can improve or worsen congestion depending on network response; integrate route choice with control rather than optimizing them separately.
use: Use for VMS, navigation guidance, incident diversion, and intelligent-agent routing.
caution: Guidance compliance and information penetration should be modeled explicitly.

authors: G. Duranton, M. A. Turner
title: The Fundamental Law of Road Congestion: Evidence from US Cities
impact: Highly cited AER empirical paper on induced traffic.
problem: Whether road expansion reduces congestion in the long run.
takeaway: Added lane-km can induce roughly proportional additional vehicle travel in the studied US context; do not evaluate expansion with fixed-demand assumptions only.
use: Use for capacity-expansion appraisal and induced-demand checks.
caution: Empirical magnitude is context-specific; do not mechanically transfer elasticity to every city or corridor.

authors: R. B. Noland, L. L. Lem
title: A Review of the Evidence for Induced Travel and Changes in Transportation and Environmental Policy in the US and the UK
venue: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment
impact: Widely cited review of induced travel.
problem: Evidence and mechanisms behind travel induced by new capacity.
takeaway: Capacity changes can trigger short-run behavioral and long-run land-use responses; forecasts should include elastic demand and scenario ranges.
use: Use for long-horizon road investment and demand forecasting.
caution: Induced travel is not identical to induced congestion; welfare and accessibility can still change positively or negatively.

authors: S. Cairns, S. Atkins, P. Goodwin
title: Disappearing Traffic? The Story So Far
venue: Proceedings of the ICE - Municipal Engineer
impact: Influential evidence synthesis on road-space reallocation.
problem: What happens when road space is removed or reassigned.
takeaway: Traffic may redistribute, retime, remode, or disappear rather than simply displacing one-for-one; evaluate behavioral adaptation instead of assuming fixed trips.
use: Use for pedestrianization, bus lanes, cycle lanes, road diets, and access restrictions.
caution: Outcomes vary substantially by alternatives, network redundancy, enforcement, and complementary measures.

authors: D. C. Shoup
title: Cruising for Parking
problem: Traffic created by drivers searching for underpriced curb parking.
takeaway: Parking management is congestion management; curb pricing and occupancy targets can remove search traffic and reduce local circulation.
use: Use for CBD congestion, curb management, school/hospital districts, and commercial streets.
caution: Pricing requires loading-zone design, enforcement, equity treatment, and off-street substitution analysis.

authors: H. Yang, M. G. H. Bell
title: Traffic Restraint, Road Pricing and Network Equilibrium
problem: How tolls can restrain demand while respecting network equilibrium.
takeaway: Toll design should be solved with network equilibrium and elastic demand; many toll patterns can meet a target, so secondary objectives matter.
use: Use for cordon, link, and area pricing design.
caution: Revenue, distribution, evasion, and political feasibility are outside pure equilibrium optimality.

authors: A. de Palma, R. Lindsey
title: Traffic Congestion Pricing Methodologies and Technologies
venue: Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies
problem: Design choices and technology options for congestion pricing.
takeaway: Pricing architecture must jointly specify spatial scope, time differentiation, vehicle classes, detection, billing, and enforcement.
use: Use for practical pricing-system design and technology selection.
caution: Operational feasibility and public acceptance can dominate theoretical first-best designs.

authors: A. Anas, R. Lindsey
title: Reducing Urban Road Transportation Externalities: Road Pricing in Theory and in Practice
venue: Review of Environmental Economics and Policy
impact: Influential policy review connecting theory and implementation.
problem: Using pricing to internalize congestion, pollution, accidents, and other externalities.
takeaway: Pricing can deliver efficiency gains, but distribution and acceptance are first-class design constraints; revenue use is part of the policy.
use: Use for policy packages and equity-aware governance.
caution: Do not evaluate pricing by travel-time savings alone.

authors: M. Liu et al.
title: Area-based Equitable Pricing Strategies for Multimodal Urban Networks with Heterogeneous Users
venue: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
problem: Balancing congestion efficiency and distributional equity among users with different values of time.
takeaway: Equity can be placed directly in the optimization objective rather than checked only after pricing is designed.
use: Use when proposing area pricing or policy packages to decision makers.
caution: Equity metric choice is normative; report who gains and loses under multiple definitions.

authors: P. B. Hunt, D. I. Robertson, R. D. Bretherton, R. I. Winton
title: SCOOT - A Traffic Responsive Method of Coordinating Signals
impact: Seminal adaptive signal-control system and field practice reference.
problem: Network coordination under changing traffic demand.
takeaway: Frequent small adjustments of split, cycle, and offset can outperform static plans when demand varies; adaptive control needs reliable detection.
use: Use as a benchmark class when comparing new signal-control algorithms.
caution: Commercial/system details and detector layouts matter; do not equate SCOOT with a generic algorithm.

authors: C. Diakaki, M. Papageorgiou, K. Aboudolas
title: A Multivariable Regulator Approach to Traffic-Responsive Network-Wide Signal Control
problem: Coordinated urban signal control under saturation.
takeaway: Queue balancing with a store-and-forward network model is a powerful oversaturation principle; prevent local queues from triggering network-wide spillback.
use: Use for congested urban networks, network-wide green split control, and benchmark design.
caution: Model aggregation suppresses detailed phase-level phenomena; calibration and constraints remain necessary.

authors: K. Aboudolas, M. Papageorgiou, E. Kosmatopoulos
title: Store-and-forward Based Methods for the Signal Control Problem in Large-Scale Congested Urban Road Networks
venue: Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies
problem: Computationally feasible control for large saturated networks.
takeaway: Balance link occupancies/queues and explicitly reduce spillback risk; computational tractability is a governance requirement for real-time deployment.
use: Use when comparing centralized optimization, feedback, and practical real-time control.
caution: Performance depends on state estimation and model structure; capacity and turning ratios should not be assumed known without evidence.

authors: K. Aboudolas, M. Papageorgiou, A. Kouvelas, E. Kosmatopoulos
title: A Rolling-Horizon Quadratic-Programming Approach to the Signal Control Problem in Large-Scale Congested Urban Road Networks
venue: Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies
impact: Influential constrained optimization approach in TR-C.
problem: Network-wide signal control with operational constraints and spillback.
takeaway: Rolling-horizon optimization can control congestion by minimizing and balancing queues, but must remain feasible at each control step.
use: Use for MPC/QP signal-control designs and Agent-generated timing policies.
caution: Prediction error and solver latency must be stress-tested.

authors: P. Varaiya
title: Max Pressure Control of a Network of Signalized Intersections
venue: Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies
problem: Decentralized network control that stabilizes queues under feasible demand.
takeaway: Serve movements with high upstream-minus-downstream pressure; downstream congestion must influence green allocation.
use: Use for oversaturated networks, decentralized control, and theoretically grounded RL reward design.
caution: Classical theory often assumes point queues/unlimited storage; finite link storage requires spillback-aware modifications.

authors: M. Papageorgiou, C. Diakaki, V. Dinopoulou, A. Kotsialos, Y. Wang
title: Review of Road Traffic Control Strategies
impact: Major highly cited review across freeway, route guidance, and urban control.
problem: Taxonomy and design principles across traffic-control strategies.
takeaway: Treat signals, ramp metering, route guidance, and information as a coordinated control system; local improvements can conflict at network scale.
use: Use as the top-level taxonomy for control-oriented governance.
caution: Technology has evolved, so pair it with recent literature for connected vehicles and learning-based control.

authors: C. F. Daganzo
title: Urban Gridlock: Macroscopic Modeling and Mitigation Approaches
problem: How oversaturated neighborhoods collapse into gridlock and how accumulation can be controlled.
takeaway: Protect critical urban regions from over-accumulation; maximizing inflow is not the same as maximizing completed trips.
use: Use for CBD protection, gating, regional control, and ITSAC network governance.
caution: A regional model needs a meaningful aggregate relation; heterogeneous congestion can weaken simple MFD assumptions.

authors: N. Geroliminis, C. F. Daganzo
title: Existence of Urban-Scale Macroscopic Fundamental Diagrams: Some Experimental Findings
problem: Whether large urban regions exhibit a stable aggregate flow-density relation.
takeaway: When a region is sufficiently homogeneous, aggregate accumulation and production can support parsimonious control; network completion rate is a better goal than isolated link speed.
use: Use to justify MFD-based monitoring and regional gating.
caution: Do not force an MFD onto highly heterogeneous networks; inspect scatter, hysteresis, and spatial variance.

authors: C. F. Daganzo, N. Geroliminis
title: An Analytical Approximation for the Macroscopic Fundamental Diagram of Urban Traffic
impact: Highly cited analytical companion to MFD experiments.
problem: When an aggregate MFD should exist and how it relates to signalized urban structure.
takeaway: Network geometry and signal timing shape aggregate capacity; MFD reasoning should be tied to network structure, not treated as a universal curve.
use: Use for analytical explanation and sensitivity analysis.
caution: Approximation assumptions may fail under severe heterogeneity, turning complexity, or nonstationary control.

authors: V. V. Gayah, C. F. Daganzo
title: Clockwise Hysteresis Loops in the Macroscopic Fundamental Diagram: An Effect of Network Instability
problem: Why network performance during congestion recovery can differ from loading.
takeaway: Spatial heterogeneity and route adaptation affect recovery; governance should reduce uneven congestion, not just average accumulation.
use: Use for recovery control, incident analysis, and interpreting MFD loops.
caution: A single average state can conceal dangerous localized oversaturation.

authors: M. Keyvan-Ekbatani, A. Kouvelas, I. Papamichail, M. Papageorgiou
title: Exploiting the Fundamental Diagram of Urban Networks for Feedback-Based Gating
impact: Highly cited bridge from MFD theory to practical gating control.
problem: Real-time protection of saturated urban regions.
takeaway: Use feedback to hold accumulation near the productive region of the MFD; perimeter signals become flow-control gates.
use: Use for real-time gating and protected-zone management.
caution: Holding vehicles outside a zone creates external queues; boundary fairness and storage must be checked.

authors: Y. Ji, N. Geroliminis
title: On the Spatial Partitioning of Urban Transportation Networks
problem: How to divide a heterogeneous city into regions suitable for MFD-based control.
takeaway: Partition by traffic-state homogeneity and spatial connectivity; control zones should be data-derived rather than administratively arbitrary.
use: Use before applying multi-region MFD or perimeter control.
caution: Partitions may need to change over time as congestion patterns evolve.

authors: M. Ramezani, J. Haddad, N. Geroliminis
title: Dynamics of Heterogeneity in Urban Networks: Aggregated Traffic Modeling and Hierarchical Control
impact: High-quality TR-B extension connecting heterogeneity and hierarchical control.
problem: Control when regional averages hide subregional imbalance.
takeaway: Use hierarchical control: regulate inter-region flows while actively reducing internal heterogeneity.
use: Use for multi-region governance and two-level controllers.
caution: Requires enough observability to estimate both accumulation and heterogeneity.

authors: M. Papageorgiou, H. Hadj-Salem, J.-M. Blosseville
title: ALINEA: A Local Feedback Control Law for On-Ramp Metering
impact: Seminal ramp-metering paper with extensive later citations and field influence.
problem: Local feedback control of freeway on-ramp inflow.
takeaway: Meter inflow to maintain downstream occupancy near a desirable set-point; simple feedback can outperform open-loop rules.
use: Use for recurrent merge bottlenecks and as a benchmark for ramp-control algorithms.
caution: Ramp storage and surface-street spillback constrain how aggressively inflow can be held.

authors: M. Papageorgiou, A. Kotsialos
title: Freeway Ramp Metering: An Overview
venue: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
problem: Why and how ramp metering mitigates recurrent and nonrecurrent congestion.
takeaway: The goal is not merely to reduce ramp inflow; it is to prevent breakdown and preserve high mainline throughput while managing queues.
use: Use for selecting local vs coordinated ramp metering.
caution: Equity and ramp-queue constraints must be included in control objectives.

authors: A. Hegyi, B. De Schutter, H. Hellendoorn
title: Model Predictive Control for Optimal Coordination of Ramp Metering and Variable Speed Limits
venue: Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies
problem: Coordinating ramp metering and variable speed limits to minimize total time spent.
takeaway: Control measures interact; optimize them jointly where possible and evaluate network total time spent rather than one detector speed.
use: Use for integrated freeway corridor management.
caution: Model mismatch, compliance with VSL, and computational requirements must be tested.

authors: M. Papageorgiou, E. Kosmatopoulos, I. Papamichail
title: Effects of Variable Speed Limits on Motorway Traffic Flow
impact: Influential empirical/control paper on VSL effects.
problem: Whether VSL improves traffic-flow efficiency as distinct from safety.
takeaway: VSL has strong safety rationale; efficiency effects depend on operating regime and should be empirically validated instead of assumed.
use: Use when recommending VSL as a congestion measure.
caution: Do not promise capacity gains without local evidence and compliance analysis.

authors: I. Papamichail, A. Kotsialos, I. Margonis, M. Papageorgiou
title: Coordinated Ramp Metering for Freeway Networks - A Model-Predictive Hierarchical Control Approach
venue: Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies
problem: Coordinated control across multiple ramps and bottlenecks.
takeaway: Combine network-level prediction/optimization with robust local feedback; hierarchical control balances global goals and local reliability.
use: Use for multi-bottleneck freeway networks.
caution: Queue limits and failure fallback policies are mandatory for deployment.

authors: M. Papageorgiou, J.-M. Blosseville, H. Hadj-Salem
title: Modelling and Real-Time Control of Traffic Flow on the Southern Part of Boulevard Périphérique in Paris: Part I: Modelling
impact: Classic field-oriented motorway modeling work underlying METANET-style control.
problem: Validated macroscopic modeling for real-time freeway control.
takeaway: Control quality depends on an operationally validated model; calibration against diverse regimes is a governance prerequisite.
use: Use for model selection and digital-twin calibration.
caution: A model that reproduces uncongested flow may still fail around breakdown and recovery.

authors: M. Eichler, C. F. Daganzo
title: Bus Lanes with Intermittent Priority: Strategy Formulae and an Evaluation
problem: How to prioritize buses without wasting road capacity when bus frequency is moderate.
takeaway: Evaluate person-delay, not vehicle-delay; intermittent priority can outperform rigid lane dedication in specific demand ranges.
use: Use for bus lanes, intermittent lanes, and arterial priority design.
caution: Not suitable near or beyond severe saturation; car-lane capacity loss can dominate.

authors: Q. He, K. L. Head, J. Ding
title: Multi-Modal Traffic Signal Control with Priority, Signal Actuation and Coordination
venue: Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies
problem: Jointly serving buses, cars, and pedestrians in coordinated signal systems.
takeaway: Priority should be conditional and network-aware; combine actuation, coordination, and multimodal priority rather than treating TSP as an isolated exception.
use: Use for corridors with buses and pedestrian constraints.
caution: Priority can transfer delay to side streets or pedestrians if person-based objectives are omitted.

authors: S. I. Guler, M. Menendez
title: Analytical Formulation and Empirical Evaluation of Pre-Signals for Bus Priority
problem: Bus priority when a dedicated lane wastes capacity.
takeaway: Upstream pre-signals can dynamically reorganize lane use and reduce person delay under suitable conditions.
use: Use for constrained urban arterials and bus approaches to signals.
caution: Geometric space, compliance, queue storage, and pedestrian interactions must be checked.

authors: S. I. Guler, V. V. Gayah, M. Menendez
title: Bus Priority at Signalized Intersections with Single-Lane Approaches: A Novel Pre-Signal Strategy
venue: Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies
problem: Providing priority when lane allocation is severely constrained.
takeaway: Evaluate operating domains where person-delay improves; priority is not universally beneficial under all saturation levels.
use: Use for single-lane approaches and dynamic lane allocation concepts.
caution: Check oversaturation and queue-blocking thresholds explicitly.

authors: Y. Lin, X. Yang, N. Zou, M. Franz
title: Transit Signal Priority Control at Signalized Intersections: A Comprehensive Review
impact: Useful comprehensive TSP review with field evidence.
problem: Taxonomy, evaluation methods, and evidence for transit signal priority.
takeaway: Separate passive, active rule-based, and model-based priority; evaluate with analytical, simulation, and field evidence.
use: Use for TSP strategy selection and literature grounding.
caution: Field benefits vary with saturation, bus frequency, schedule adherence, and coordination.

authors: H. Wei et al.
title: PressLight: Learning Max Pressure Control for Signalized Intersections in Arterial Network
impact: Highly influential bridge between traffic-control theory and deep RL.
problem: Designing RL state/reward using traffic theory rather than heuristics.
takeaway: Theory-informed rewards can improve learning stability; use pressure/queue structure instead of arbitrary reward engineering.
use: Use for RL signal-control agents and ITSAC innovation sections.
caution: Simulation superiority does not imply field robustness; benchmark against non-learning controllers and test distribution shift.

authors: H. Wei et al.
title: CoLight: Learning Network-Level Cooperation for Traffic Signal Control
problem: Learning cooperation across many signalized intersections.
takeaway: Communication topology matters; graph-based information sharing is a natural representation for networked signals.
use: Use for multi-agent RL and graph-based signal coordination.
caution: Scalability in simulation does not guarantee transferability, safety, interpretability, or field communications reliability.

authors: H. Wei, G. Zheng, V. Gayah, Z. Li
title: Recent Advances in Reinforcement Learning for Traffic Signal Control: A Survey of Models and Evaluation
problem: How RL-TSC methods differ in state, action, reward, coordination, and evaluation.
takeaway: Evaluation design is as important as model novelty; compare against strong transportation baselines and report simulator assumptions.
use: Use for experiment design and avoiding weak baselines.
caution: Survey predates the newest foundation-model/large-scale multi-agent work; supplement with recent reviews.

authors: Various authors
title: Reinforcement Learning in Urban Network Traffic Signal Control: A Systematic Literature Review
impact: Large systematic review covering 160 peer-reviewed network-level studies through March 2020.
problem: Evidence quality and research trends in network-level RL signal control.
takeaway: The field has reproducibility, benchmark, and practitioner-integration gaps; governance should not treat simulated RL gains as field-proven.
use: Use for methodological caveats and research-gap sections.
caution: Systematic-review inclusion window means newer methods require separate updates.

authors: Y. Han, M. Wang, L. Leclercq
title: Leveraging Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Traffic Control: A Survey and Challenges for Field Implementation
problem: Why RL traffic control struggles to move from simulation to deployment.
takeaway: Sim-to-real transfer, safety, data cost, nonstationarity, and operational constraints must be designed in from the start.
use: Use for modern Agent/RL governance and field-deployment checklists.
caution: Use RL only when it beats simpler robust methods under realistic disturbances and constraints.

authors: J. Yoon, K. Ahn, J. Park, H. Yeo
title: Transferable Traffic Signal Control: Reinforcement Learning with Graph Centric State Representation
venue: Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies
problem: Generalizing signal-control policies to unseen demand states.
takeaway: Representation design can improve transfer, but robustness should be measured across demand, topology, detector noise, and incident scenarios.
use: Use when claiming an Agent can generalize beyond one calibrated simulation.
caution: Transferability claims are bounded by tested domains; do not extrapolate silently.

authors: M. Papageorgiou
title: An Integrated Control Approach for Traffic Corridors
venue: Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies
problem: Coordinating signals, ramp metering, route guidance, and other controls under one objective.
takeaway: Optimize corridor controls jointly around total delay/time spent; isolated controllers can fight each other.
use: Use for integrated corridor management and multi-tool Agents.
caution: Joint optimization increases model and operational complexity; define fallback modes.

authors: R. Z. Farahani, E. Miandoabchi, W. Y. Szeto, H. Rashidi
title: A Review of Urban Transportation Network Design Problems
problem: How road and public-transport network design problems are formulated and solved.
takeaway: Network design is inherently bilevel/multilevel: infrastructure decisions change route/mode choices; evaluate equilibrium response and multiple objectives.
use: Use for long-term governance and network redesign.
caution: Design-optimal solutions can be politically or operationally infeasible; add implementability constraints.

authors: F. Ahmed, Y. E. Hawas
title: An Integrated Real-Time Traffic Signal System for Transit Signal Priority, Incident Detection and Congestion Management
venue: Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies
problem: Handling recurrent congestion, incidents, downstream blockage, and transit priority in one signal system.
takeaway: Governance logic should identify operating regime first; the best control action differs between recurrent congestion, incidents, and downstream blockage.
use: Use for rule-based Agent state machines and incident-aware signal control.
caution: Simulation validation should be complemented with field data before deployment claims.

authors: T. L. Friesz, D. Bernstein, T. E. Smith, R. L. Tobin, B. W. Wie
title: A Variational Inequality Formulation of the Dynamic Network User Equilibrium Problem
impact: Seminal dynamic user-equilibrium formulation in a top OR journal.
problem: Dynamic route and departure-time equilibrium with FIFO.
takeaway: Traffic-management policies should be evaluated against time-dependent route/departure responses, not only a static assignment.
use: Use for dynamic route guidance, event traffic, time-varying pricing, DTA and diversion evaluation.
caution: The formulation is theoretical; operational deployment needs a calibrated dynamic network loading model.

authors: S. Peeta, A. K. Ziliaskopoulos
title: Foundations of Dynamic Traffic Assignment: The Past, the Present and the Future
impact: Canonical review of dynamic traffic assignment.
problem: How DTA formulations connect mathematical programming, optimal control, VI and simulation.
takeaway: Use DTA when congestion management changes route choice over time and queue propagation matters.
use: Use as a map of DTA concepts before selecting a route-guidance or network-control model.
caution: A review is not an operational algorithm; choose a specific DNL and equilibrium concept for implementation.

authors: B. W. Wie, T. L. Friesz, R. L. Tobin
title: Dynamic User Optimal Traffic Assignment on Congested Multidestination Networks
impact: Early influential dynamic user-optimal assignment paper in TR-B.
problem: Dynamic generalization of Wardrop equilibrium for congested multi-OD networks.
takeaway: Diversion and information policies can produce new time-dependent equilibria; evaluate the resulting state, not the first-order rerouting response.
use: Use for route guidance, peak management and network diversion reasoning.
caution: Continuous-time optimal-control assumptions are idealized and require practical approximations.

authors: J. Eliasson
title: A Cost-Benefit Analysis of the Stockholm Congestion Charging System
venue: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
impact: Highly influential observed-data evaluation of congestion charging.
problem: Whether a real congestion-pricing scheme generates net social benefits.
takeaway: Judge pricing with observed traffic, travel time, revenue, operating cost, safety and emissions rather than traffic reduction alone.
use: Use when designing pricing evaluation and benefit-cost evidence.
caution: Transferability depends on geography, alternatives, charge design, implementation cost and public finance.

authors: J. Eliasson, L. Hultkrantz, L. Nerhagen, L. Smidfelt Rosqvist
title: The Stockholm Congestion-Charging Trial 2006: Overview of Effects
venue: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
problem: Observed network and public-response effects of a time-differentiated cordon charge.
takeaway: A policy trial can change both congestion and acceptance; visible travel-time reliability gains matter for legitimacy.
use: Use for cordon pricing, pilot design, public acceptance and before-after evaluation.
caution: Do not assume the same acceptance trajectory where transit alternatives or governance conditions differ.

authors: J. Leape
title: The London Congestion Charge
impact: Widely cited policy account in a leading economics journal.
problem: How central London implemented congestion charging and what effects followed.
takeaway: Implementation design, exemptions, enforcement and political feasibility are part of traffic governance, not afterthoughts.
use: Use for policy narratives, implementation constraints and charge-zone governance.
caution: A city-center charging case should not be copied mechanically to polycentric cities.

authors: R. Arnott, E. Inci
title: An Integrated Model of Downtown Parking and Traffic Congestion
problem: How underpriced curb parking creates cruising traffic and congestion.
takeaway: Parking price and occupancy are traffic-control variables; curb search traffic should be included in congestion diagnosis.
use: Use for CBD parking pricing, curb management and search-traffic mitigation.
caution: Simplified downtown assumptions require local occupancy, turnover and search behavior data.

authors: R. Arnott, J. Rowse
title: Downtown Parking in Auto City
problem: Joint effects of curb parking, garage parking, cruising and downtown traffic.
takeaway: Treat curb and off-street parking as a coupled market; changing one price can shift search and occupancy elsewhere.
use: Use for district parking portfolios rather than isolated curb-price changes.
caution: Stylized equilibrium results need empirical validation before operational target setting.

authors: A. G. Sims, K. W. Dobinson
title: The Sydney Coordinated Adaptive Traffic (SCAT) System Philosophy and Benefits
impact: Classic adaptive traffic-control system paper; several hundred indexed citations.
problem: Network-adaptive signal timing using traffic-responsive cycle, split and offset logic.
takeaway: Adaptive control is an operations system involving detection, coordination logic and fallback plans, not just an optimizer.
use: Use as a classical benchmark family and for deployment architecture reasoning.
caution: SCATS is a system architecture; do not reduce it to one formula or compare with RL using incompatible detectors/KPIs.

authors: N. H. Gartner
title: OPAC: A Demand-Responsive Strategy for Traffic Signal Control
impact: Classic demand-responsive decentralized signal-control work; heavily cited.
problem: Real-time demand-responsive optimization with upstream detector input.
takeaway: Rolling local optimization can be practical when it uses available detector data and decomposes network control.
use: Use for adaptive signal-control lineage and decentralized optimization baselines.
caution: Reported performance depends on detector quality and prediction horizon; historical implementations differ from modern systems.

authors: P. Mirchandani, L. Head
title: A Real-Time Traffic Signal Control System: Architecture, Algorithms, and Analysis
venue: Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies
problem: Hierarchical prediction and control across vehicle/platoon/network resolutions.
takeaway: Good adaptive control architecture separates prediction, local decisions and network coordination by time scale.
use: Use when designing hierarchical Agent/tool architectures for signal control.
caution: Prediction accuracy and computation deadlines are part of the control problem.

authors: J. D. C. Little, M. D. Kelson, N. H. Gartner
title: MAXBAND: A Program for Setting Signals on Arteries and Triangular Networks
impact: Classic arterial progression / bandwidth optimization reference.
problem: Choosing cycle, offsets and progression bands for coordinated arterials.
takeaway: When the main objective is progression, optimize corridor coordination explicitly rather than only intersection delay.
use: Use for arterial coordination baselines and offset-plan design.
caution: Bandwidth objectives can disadvantage cross streets, pedestrians or oversaturated conditions; pair with demand/capacity constraints.

authors: T. Wongpiromsarn, T. Uthaicharoenpong, Y. Wang, E. Frazzoli, D. Wang
title: Distributed Traffic Signal Control for Maximum Network Throughput
impact: Important bridge from backpressure theory to distributed signal control.
problem: Distributed signal control with maximum-throughput guarantees.
takeaway: Pressure-based decentralized control can offer strong theoretical baselines for congested networks and should be compared before claiming ML gains.
use: Use as a baseline and theoretical anchor for decentralized/agent signal control.
caution: Throughput optimality assumptions do not automatically guarantee good pedestrian service, fairness or finite-storage performance.

authors: H. K. Lo
title: A Novel Traffic Signal Control Formulation
venue: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
problem: Joint representation of signal control and traffic assignment/dynamics.
takeaway: Signal timing changes route/network states; optimization should reflect the traffic response to control rather than freeze demand patterns.
use: Use for signal-control formulations with network interactions.
caution: Model complexity and solution tractability limit direct real-time deployment.

authors: M. J. Cassidy, J. Rudjanakanoknad
title: Increasing the Capacity of an Isolated Merge by Metering Its On-Ramp
problem: Whether metering can restore higher discharge flow at an active merge bottleneck.
takeaway: Ramp metering can protect the bottleneck from breakdown; queue location and lane-changing mechanism matter as much as average demand.
use: Use for merge bottlenecks, capacity drop and ramp-metering rationale.
caution: A successful isolated-merge experiment does not guarantee network-wide gains if ramp queues spill back to surface streets.

authors: G. Gomes, R. Horowitz
title: Optimal Freeway Ramp Metering Using the Asymmetric Cell Transmission Model
venue: Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies
problem: Constrained optimal metering with mainline congestion and ramp queue limits.
takeaway: Operational constraints such as maximum ramp queues belong inside the optimization, not in post-processing.
use: Use for CTM-based freeway control and constrained ramp-metering design.
caution: Results rely on model structure and conditions preventing problematic queue propagation; validate with realistic demand uncertainty.

authors: C. F. Daganzo, J. Laval, J. C. Muñoz
title: Ten Strategies for Freeway Congestion Mitigation with Advanced Technologies
problem: Which operational strategies can mitigate freeway congestion without relying on large infrastructure expansion.
takeaway: Prefer strategies that target breakdown, lane interactions, bottleneck activation and demand peaking and that can be evaluated with observable KPIs.
use: Use as a mechanism checklist when generating freeway interventions.
caution: It is a research report and strategy framework, not a current design standard.

authors: E. Smaragdis, M. Papageorgiou, E. Kosmatopoulos
title: A Flow-Maximizing Adaptive Local Ramp Metering Strategy
problem: How to maximize mainstream flow with local feedback under changing traffic.
takeaway: Local feedback can be strengthened with bottleneck-flow objectives, but queue constraints and network interactions remain essential.
use: Use as a classical adaptive-metering comparator.
caution: Local objectives may transfer congestion to ramps or adjacent links if not coordinated.

authors: J. Hu, B. B. Park, Y.-J. Lee
title: Coordinated Transit Signal Priority Supporting Transit Progression under Connected Vehicle Technology
venue: Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies
impact: Influential connected-vehicle TSP / corridor coordination paper.
problem: How to preserve bus priority benefits across consecutive signals.
takeaway: Transit priority should be corridor-coordinated and preferably person-delay-aware rather than granting isolated priority at each junction.
use: Use for connected-bus priority and multimodal corridor control.
caution: Benefits decrease under heavy saturation; protect general-traffic storage and downstream capacity.

authors: W. Ma, X. Yang, Y. Liu
title: Development and Evaluation of a Coordinated and Conditional Bus Priority Approach
problem: How to coordinate priority for early/late buses across intersection groups.
takeaway: Conditional priority can improve reliability with smaller side effects than unconditional priority; schedule/headway state should influence grants.
use: Use for bus-reliability governance and priority logic design.
caution: Transfer requires accurate bus prediction and local signal constraints.

authors: J. Hu, B. B. Park, A. E. Parkany
title: Transit Signal Priority with Connected Vehicle Technology
problem: How two-way bus-signal communication and passenger data can improve TSP.
takeaway: Reallocate rather than simply add green, and consider person delay / passenger count when prioritizing transit.
use: Use for multimodal signal KPIs and connected transit priority.
caution: Connected-vehicle penetration and communication assumptions must be explicit.

authors: H. Wei, G. Zheng, H. Yao, Z. Li
title: IntelliLight: A Reinforcement Learning Approach for Intelligent Traffic Light Control
impact: Early influential deep-RL traffic-signal paper at KDD.
problem: Learning adaptive single-intersection control from traffic state.
takeaway: Use real/realistic demand, interpretable state/reward design and strong transport baselines when evaluating RL.
use: Use to understand early deep-RL TSC design choices.
caution: Do not infer field superiority from offline/simulation performance alone.

authors: G. Zheng, Y. Xiong, X. Zang, J. Feng, H. Wei, H. Zhang, Y. Li, K. Xu, Z. Li
title: Learning Phase Competition for Traffic Signal Control
impact: Influential FRAP paper; strong inductive-bias approach for RL signal control.
problem: Generalizable all-phase selection under changing flow and intersection geometry.
takeaway: Embedding traffic-control structure and symmetry can improve sample efficiency and transfer compared with generic neural policies.
use: Use for RL architecture design and generalization discussions.
caution: Generalization still depends on simulator fidelity, demand distribution and action constraints.

authors: X. Zang, H. Yao, G. Zheng, N. Xu, K. Xu, Z. Li
title: MetaLight: Value-Based Meta-Reinforcement Learning for Traffic Signal Control
impact: Influential meta-RL traffic-signal paper at AAAI.
problem: Fast adaptation to new traffic scenarios using experience from prior scenarios.
takeaway: Transfer/adaptation should be treated as a first-class deployment requirement; training from scratch for every junction is not a practical governance plan.
use: Use for domain adaptation and rapid reconfiguration discussions.
caution: Meta-training distribution can still mismatch deployment; require out-of-distribution stress tests.

authors: H. Zhang, S. Feng, C. Liu, Y. Ding, Y. Zhu, Z. Zhou, W. Zhang, Y. Yu, H. Jin, Z. Li
title: CityFlow: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Environment for Large Scale City Traffic Scenario
impact: Widely used large-scale traffic-signal RL simulation environment paper.
problem: Scalable simulation for large multi-agent traffic-control experiments.
takeaway: Simulation infrastructure affects conclusions; benchmark claims need reproducible network, demand, seed and simulator settings.
use: Use for experimental design and RL benchmark reproducibility.
caution: Simulator speed is not simulator validity; calibrate behavioral and flow properties to the target setting.

authors: S. El-Tantawy, B. Abdulhai, H. Abdelgawad
title: Multiagent Reinforcement Learning for Integrated Network of Adaptive Traffic Signal Controllers (MARLIN-ATSC): Methodology and Large-Scale Application on Downtown Toronto
venue: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
impact: Highly cited multi-agent RL signal-control paper in IEEE T-ITS.
problem: Coordinated multi-agent learning across a large urban signal network.
takeaway: Coordination can outperform independent agents, but network-scale validation and communication design are necessary.
use: Use as an early large-network MARL reference and comparison point.
caution: Simulation-network results require careful baseline tuning and field-transfer analysis.

authors: H. Mei, X. Lei, L. Da, B. Shi, H. Wei
title: LibSignal: An Open Library for Traffic Signal Control
impact: Useful reproducibility benchmark for cross-simulator TSC comparison.
problem: Fair implementation and comparison of signal-control methods across simulators.
takeaway: A governance Agent should prefer unified datasets, metrics, seeds and simulator calibration before ranking algorithms.
use: Use to define benchmarking protocol rather than as evidence that one method universally wins.
caution: Preprint/library evidence is method-infrastructure evidence, not field deployment evidence.
